summary: Colma's population of roughly 1,400 living residents is vastly outnumbered by the estimated 1.5 million buried beneath it — the town became a necropolis in the early twentieth century when San Francisco banned new burials and cemeteries migrated south, making this tiny 1.9-square-mile municipality one of the most unusual incorporated cities in the United States. That history shapes the landscape today: much of the acreage is occupied by sprawling, manicured memorial parks rather than housing tracts, which is partly why the density sits at just 748 people per square mile despite being wedged between Daly City and South San Francisco on the Peninsula. The property crime rate per capita looks staggering — over 70,000 per 100K — but with only ~1,400 residents and a large commercial strip anchored by a major auto mall and big-box retail drawing regional traffic, the per-resident math inflates dramatically; the zero homicides recorded reinforces that the raw numbers need context. A median home value above $1 million against a median household income of about $121,500 yields a price-to-income ratio north of 8.5, meaning purchasing requires substantial savings or equity beyond local earnings alone, while median rent near $2,150 consumes roughly 21% of that median income — comparatively manageable for the Bay Area. The climate is classic coastal San Mateo County: average highs around 63°F year-round, fog-cooled summers, and mild winters with minimal temperature swings, offering 8.4 hours of daily sunshine that often arrives after the morning marine layer burns off. BART's Colma station provides a direct rail link into San Francisco and through to the East Bay, making it functional as a commuter base despite having almost no major employers beyond retail and cemetery operations within its borders. Colma is a place defined by a genuinely strange duality — a living town built around the business of the dead, offering Bay Area proximity and transit access at a slightly lower rent burden, but with almost no walkable residential fabric of its own.
